question_text: What is the characteristic called in the programme, and what does the name signal about its essential nature?

sample.text: **[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic is named "Moral-inner defilement-state." Three elements of the name are analytically significant. *Moral*: the defilement is located in the moral domain — it concerns the inner person's orientation toward good, evil, right, and wrong, not merely a ritual or bodily condition. *Inner*: the locus is the interior of the person — conscience, will, heart — not external contact or authoritative verdict (that is Characteristic 1). *Defilement-state*: it is a condition, not an act — the person is in a state of corruption, not merely performing corrupt acts. The name signals that this characteristic is the inner-being condition of a morally compromised interior, which the evidence confirms: Mat 23:27 (VCG-04) — "within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness"; Eph 4:19 (VCG-02) — "greedy to practice every kind of impurity" arising from a silenced conscience.

The cluster is named "Blessing, Favour and Grace" (the cluster description). Within the programme, M39-A carries the sub-group label "Blessing and Grace." The name reveals: (1) "Blessing" names the comprehensive act — the sovereign declaration that constitutes flourishing (ba.rakh as the dominant OT term); (2) "Grace" names the inner disposition and relational mode — the freely given, unmerited quality of the characteristic (charis/chen/charitoō); (3) "Favour" bridges them — the relational standing that blessing produces and grace constitutes. Together the name signals that the characteristic is at once an act (blessing), a disposition (grace), and a relational outcome (favour).

The characteristic is called 'love' — a name that in English collapses a vocabulary of multiple Hebrew and Greek terms into a single referent. The name signals an orientation outward: love is always toward something or someone; it cannot be self-contained. Even the word's grammar in Scripture consistently requires a direct object (love of God, love of neighbour, love of enemy, love of money). The name also signals relational constitution: the one who loves is partly constituted by who and what they love. The programme's description note ('most foundational and most theologically dense word in the entire corpus,' OBS-103-004) signals that the name functions as an organising category for the entire inner-being vocabulary.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Habitual defection." The name encodes two claims. (1) *Habitual*: the characteristic is not a single act but a pattern settled over time — the will's default direction has been established toward sin. This contrasts with CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning — single act) and CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent — the decision-point of non-departure). The habit dimension signals that the sinning has moved beyond the episodic into the dispositional: it is the will's natural default rather than a departure from it. (2) *Defection*: the sinning is a going-away-from, an abandonment of loyalty — the image of someone who was in or should be in a covenant relationship but has repeatedly moved away from it. 2Ki 17:7 — "sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt" — the redemptive background makes the sinning a defection: they were brought out, they have defected back. The name signals: a formed inner orientation of departure from God, not merely occasional sin but the will's settled direction.

Anxiety and Worry. The name signals both the affective dimension (anxiety — the felt state of distress) and the cognitive-behavioural dimension (worry — the repetitive mental engagement with anticipated threat). The conjunction "and" acknowledges the duality within a single sub-group.

question_text: What do the primary Hebrew and Greek terms show at the definitional level?

sample.text:
Five terms covering different registers:
- **H2781 cher.pah** — the dominant term (72 verses); reproach, disgrace, taunt, insult. Operates across individual and corporate levels with the same word — from "reproaches have broken my heart" (Psa 69:20) to "I will make you a desolation and an object of reproach among the nations" (Eze 5:14).
- **H5007A ne.a.tsah** — disgrace as an inner condition in extremity (2Ki 19:3); the acute overwhelming shame-experience when crisis produces incapacity.
- **H8146 sa.ni** — the disfavoured/unloved; chronic relational condition of being the less-loved spouse with legal consequences (Deu 21:15).
- **H8103 shim.tsah** — derision; the mocking contempt of enemies (Exo 32:25).
- **G5195 hubrizō** — to mistreat shamefully; insolent treatment that violates the person's dignity. More agentive than cher.pah: it names the act of the one who mistreats.

distazō (Greek): from dis (twice, double) — to be of two minds, to waver. dipsuchos: dis (double) + psuchē (soul) — two-souled. The Greek terms for both doubt and double-mindedness carry the same "double/division" root structure — unifying the sub-group at the etymological level around inner division.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Four primary Greek terms carry this characteristic. ponēros (G4190, 63V): the most comprehensive term — spanning evil as a quality of persons, deeds, thoughts, and cosmic powers; at root it names what is characteristically bad or corrupt in a moral sense. kakia (G2549, 11V): specifically names settled inner badness — malice, ill-will, wickedness as an entrenched inner residue; the term's usage in Eph 4:31 (VCG-05), Col 3:8 (VCG-05), 1Pe 2:1 (VCG-05) consistently addresses it as something deeply seated requiring deliberate stripping off. adikia (G0093, 8V): unrighteousness — the condition of being structurally not-right, especially in relation to moral and legal norms; Rom 1:18 (VCG-05) names it as actively suppressing truth. ponēria (G4189, 7V): wickedness, villainy — typically naming active malicious intent; Mar 7:22 (VCG-05) lists it as an inner vice emerging from the heart. faulos (G5337, 1V): a term for what is cheap, bad, or worthless — applied to deeds in 2Cor 5:10 (VCG-06). Collectively the terms map evil across quality (ponēros), residual badness (kakia), structural wrongness (adikia), active malice (ponēria), and evaluative worthlessness (faulos).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary Hebrew: to.e.vah (H8441, ~35V in this characteristic) — the term names that which is ritually or morally abhorrent; its root may connect to a verb of loathing or turning away in disgust. At the definitional level, to.e.vah designates a category of violation so severe that it provokes active revulsion rather than mere disapproval. The term is consistently relational — "an abomination to the Lord" or "to the righteous" — signalling that abomination is defined in relationship (the revulsion of the other), not self-referentially. Primary Greek: bdelugma (G0946, 4V — Luk 16:15; Rev 17:4; 17:5; 21:27) — from bdeo, to stink; the root names what is repugnant through its putrid, offensive quality. bdeluktos (G0947, 1V — Tit 1:16) — the adjectival form: the detestable or loathsome person. The Greek root's derivation from the concept of stench adds a sensory-disgust dimension: abomination is that which morally stinks in the divine nostrils.

The primary Hebrew terms operate in four registers at first encounter. Material-state terms (o.sher, hon, cho.sen — riches, substance, wealth) name the condition of having material goods, with no intrinsic moral valence. Process terms (a.shar — to become rich; da.shen — to prosper/grow fat; sha.men verb — to grow fat) name the dynamic of material acquisition or increase, again without intrinsic moral valence but loaded with contextual moral weight. Inner-state terms (sha.a.nan — at ease/complacent; autarkēs — self-sufficient/content; cha.san — to hoard) name specific inner orientations in relation to material circumstance. Person-type terms (a.shir, plousios — the rich person; ptōchos — the poor person) name the social-moral category of persons defined by their material condition. The Greek terms (plousios, ploutos, plouteō, ploutizō, ptōchos, ptōcheuō) follow the same fourfold pattern but with the additional NT theological loading: plousios in Rev 3:17 and ptōchos in Mat 5:3 both carry inner-being extensions that exceed their Greek economic senses.

question_text: What directional, relational, or constitutional implication does the name carry?

sample.text: **[CHAR-15]** E — All three. *Directional*: the condition moves backward (from ancestors to present) and forward (from present to descendants); Isa 43:27's "first father sinned" is the backward direction; the ongoing pattern (Psa 78:17/32 — still sinning) is the forward continuation. *Relational*: the condition is constitutively relational — it operates within lineages, families, and covenant communities; it cannot be inherited without the relational bond of ancestry. *Constitutional*: Isa 64:5 — "in our sins we have been a long time" — the prolonged duration suggests the condition has become constitutional, not merely episodic.

Constitutional: both terms (distazō, dipsuchos) carry division within the self as the constitutional implication — the self is not unified.

The vocabulary confirms this — aphiēmi (send away, release) moves the debt away from the relational field. The direction is consistently *from* one who holds a claim *toward* one who owes it.

The name and vocabulary together imply: a wrong done, a claim registered, a relationship under strain, and the act that addresses the strain. Constitutional: "evil generation" places the characteristic at the generative heart of the person — in the heart (Isa 32:6 — vc=38181 — VCG-02: "heart is busy with iniquity") and in the thought-life (Isa 59:7 — vc=38203 — VCG-02: "their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity"). question_text: What kind of inner-being phenomenon is the characteristic — an act, a disposition, a condition/status, a quality, or something else?

sample.text: **[G — Structural Opposites]** Condition — the state of being wicked or unjust. Ra.sha and a.val name what a person is (ra.sha: the wicked one) and what they do, but the consistent use of ra.sha as a person-type identifies the primary character as conditional — a governing state of the person.

M46-D contains both acts and dispositions. Poverty of spirit (Mat 5:3) names a disposition — the stable inner posture of dependence before God. The voluntary release (Gen 14:23; Luk 19:8; 2Cor 8:9) names inner acts — specific choices to relinquish wealth. Learned contentment (autarkēs, Phil 4:11) names an achieved disposition — the stable inner settledness that has been formed through experience. M46-D is the most complex sub-group in terms of inner-being kind: it holds posture, act, and achieved disposition in a unified frame.

Primarily a disposition — a stable inner orientation toward another — that generates states and acts. Three levels: (a) God's chesed "never ceases" — a permanent attribute, not episodic act [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-085]; (b) Pro 3:3 — chesed written on the heart — heart-inscription is the language of stable inner character [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-087]; (c) H2623 — the chasid names the person characterised by chesed — a dispositional identity, not an occasional actor [XREG: H2623, OBS-099-094]. Acts of kindness (Ruth, David, chrēsteuomai) are expressions of the underlying disposition.
Mixed: distazō is a momentary condition (doubt arising in a specific encounter); dipsuchos is a dispositional quality (the settled state of the double-minded person).

The definition tier (T1) positions contrition as a threshold event (not an end-state but a passage toward divine response); the formative tier (T5) confirms and extends this by showing that contrition's productive function is precisely its threshold character — it is the recurring event through which the person is returned to receptivity. T1's sequence (crushing → contrite posture → divine response) maps directly onto T5's formative arc (dissolution-through-encounter → contrite state → character of lowliness formed through repeated cycles). The definitional claim that contrition is a passage rather than a terminal state (T1) is confirmed by T5's formation account: the sustainable inner posture produced is not permanent brokenness but the characterological lowliness that emerges from repeated breaking-and-reviving.

question_text: Is the characteristic simple in structure, or does it combine constituent elements; if compound, which?

sample.text: **[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 is complex in structure. The seat-of-pride axis that generated the four sub-groups (M08-A1 through M08-A4) is itself evidence of internal differentiation within a single characteristic: the same inner movement of self-elevation is named through the heart (Pro 16:5, vc=12083, M08-A1-VCG-03: "arrogant in heart"), the eyes (Pro 6:17, vc=34247, M08-A2-VCG-01: "haughty eyes"), the national/collective register (Isa 16:6, vc=33989, M08-A3-VCG-01: "we have heard of the pride of Moab"), and the general dispositional form (Pro 16:18, vc=34073; Rom 1:30, vc=33932, M08-A4-VCG-01). Within the sub-groups, further constituent registers appear: prosperity-triggered elevation (M08-A1-VCG-01: Deu 8:14, Hos 13:6), royal power elevation (M08-A1-VCG-02: Eze 28:2, Dan 11:36), volitional self-assertion against God (M08-A4-VCG-05: Isa 14:13, Num 15:30), and the self-love root that generates the whole (M08-A4-VCG-01: 2Ti 3:2, vc=1899: filautos). CHAR-1 has constituent elements — triggers, sub-registers, and generative roots — while remaining a single characteristic identity.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The corpus reveals two constituent elements. (1) *Passive non-departure*: the majority of the Kings corpus — "did not depart," "did not turn aside" — presents the characteristic as a failure to move, a remaining-in-place. The will does not actively turn toward sin but fails to turn away from it. (2) *Active clinging and hardening*: 2Ki 3:3 — "he *clung* to the sin of Jeroboam" — the will actively adheres to the sinful course; Neh 9:29 — "stubborn shoulder... stiffened their neck... *would not* obey" — active wilful resistance to turning. The two constituent elements (passive non-departure vs active clinging/resistance) represent different intensities of the same refusal: from staying put (passive) to gripping and resisting (active).

M01-C and D are relatively simple in structure — terror-as-force has the constituent elements of source (external) and recipient (inner person), but this is structural rather than constituent in the sense of M01-A. M01-D's dismay appears simple: disruption → collapse.

The cluster is constitutively complex. At first encounter from the gloss list (abundance, be poor, be rich, fatness, poor, rich, riches, richly, secure, self-sufficient, substance, to enrich, to grow fat, to hoard, to luxuriate, to prosper, wealth) the vocabulary spans states, processes, persons, and orientations — no single simple structure. The four sub-groups are themselves the analytical answer to this complexity: M46 is not one inner-being phenomenon but a domain in which four distinct inner-being phenomena (inner closure, hardness and insatiability, ordering of character and wealth, life beyond material circumstance) operate, each with its own structure.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence evidences two constituent elements. First, the *calibrated-restraint element* (metriopatheō — Heb5:2): the capacity to hold force, judgment, or severity in measured response — not to go to excess in either direction. Second, the *volitional-readiness element* (okneō — Act9:38): the absence of resistant hesitation — the inner freedom that does not create friction between perceiving a genuine need and responding to it. These are distinguishable: one can have calibrated gentleness without instant responsiveness (the gentle person who nevertheless delays); or volitional readiness without calibrated gentleness (the person who responds immediately but without measured compassion). Together they define the full characteristic.

question_text: What stands against the characteristic as its structural opposite — the inner-being reality that excludes it?

sample.text: **[F — Moral Reckoning]** Corrupt assessment — the failure to reckon honestly. More precisely, reckoning without grounding in faith (Rom 14:23: "whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith"). Reckoning without faith-grounding produces the wrong conclusion and the wrong action.

The structural opposite of inner closure is inner perceptiveness and openness — the person who sees, hears, understands, and turns (Isa 6:10 uses these four as what fat-heartedness prevents). VCG01 (2Cor 4:4 anchor): blinded minds — thought-content capacity sealed from light. The opposite is blindness/captivity of thought-content.

Compassion — the inner disposition that takes pain in another's suffering rather than pleasure. The compound opposite: solidarity rather than enmity, recognition of worth rather than contempt, sorrow at harm rather than joy.

Courage (tharseō), perseverance, the parakaleō (encouragement) that restores the fainthearted. Within the VCG evidence: 2Cor 4:16 names it — the inner person being renewed day by day as the opposite of losing heart.

question_text: Does the characteristic operate through a communicative or speech-based mode (commanded, addressed, spoken); if so, how? Record it, or record none.

sample.text: **[CHAR-4]** E — Indirectly. The high priest's "dealing gently with the ignorant and wayward" (Heb5:2 — metriopatheō) almost certainly involves speech in its mediation — the priestly mediation between erring people and God involves verbal intercession and instruction. The gentleness of the engagement is carried partly through the manner and tone of speech. Act9:38 involves speech explicitly ("urging him, 'Please come to us without delay'") — but the speech here is the disciples' communication, not Peter's; the okneō named is the absence of the quality that would prevent prompt response. The characteristic shapes the manner of speech (the metriopatheō quality) without being a purely speech-constituted characteristic.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows a limited but real speech-adjacent mode. In the ka.na corpus, the outward expression of the inner humbling is often paired with speech-acts: 2Ch12:6 — the princes "humble themselves and said, 'The Lord is righteous'" — verbal acknowledgment of God's rightness is the expression of the inner act. 2Ki22:19 and 2Ch34:27 pair the humbling with weeping and tearing clothes (embodied expression) but also with the act of receiving God's spoken word as addressed to oneself. The characteristic does not primarily operate through speech but it regularly issues in speech-acts of acknowledgment (confession, praise, verbal self-lowering) and is itself awakened by the reception of spoken word (God's address through the prophets). 2Cor10:1 (Paul's self-effacement in personal presence) suggests the characteristic also shapes the manner and register of speech rather than its content alone.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Speech-adjacent modes are present in four of the six characteristics; two are silent on this. CHAR-1 Humility: speech-adjacent — the humbling is expressed in verbal acknowledgment of God's rightness (2Ch12:6 — "the Lord is righteous") and in receiving God's word as personally claiming. CHAR-2 Submission: auditory-constitutive — the very root of hupakoē is "under-hearing"; the characteristic is constituted by reception-and-yielding to what is heard. CHAR-4 Meekness: indirectly speech-involved — the high priest's gentle dealing (Heb5:2) involves verbal intercession and instruction. CHAR-5 Dignity: directly speech-shaping — Tit2:7 ("in your teaching show… dignity") — the manner of teaching is the characteristic's communicative expression. CHAR-3 Contrition and CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness are silent on communicative modes in their direct evidence. Cluster-level: CHAR-2's auditory-constitutive character (hupakoē — under-hearing) makes it unique in the cluster — it is the only characteristic whose very root encodes reception of heard speech as its constitutional origin. CHAR-5's communicative mode (teaching manner) makes it unique as the characteristic most directly expressed in and through verbal instruction.

---

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the cry for justice is the primary communicative mode of D. "Give me justice against my adversary" (Luk 18:3, VSG 944-001) is speech directed toward God. The cry is not mere complaint — it is an inner act of faith directed toward the God who will answer.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Yes — in three speech-modes. (1) *Confession*: Lev 16:21 — "Aaron shall confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel" — the verbal act of naming iniquity over the scapegoat; Psa 38:18 — "I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin"; Lev 26:40 — "if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers"; (2) *Self-accusation*: Jer 14:7 — "though our iniquities testify against us" — iniquity is personified as a witness speaking against the person in God's court; (3) *Denial*: Hos 12:8 — "they cannot find in me iniquity or sin" — the self-deceived conscience's speech-denial of existing iniquity; Job 31:33 — "if I have concealed my transgressions... by hiding my iniquity in my heart" — the alternative is named as speech-concealment.

question_text: What first or most immediate inner-being response does this verse show following the characteristic? Record it, or record none.

sample.text: **[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence addresses two distinct immediate-response patterns. From the perspective of the one who perceives abomination in another: Eze 9:4 (vc=1698 — VCG-04) shows the immediate response as sighing and groaning — a conscience-driven, grief-laden inner recoil at encountered abomination. Pro 29:27 (vc=65959 — VCG-01): "an unjust man is an abomination to the righteous" — the righteous person's immediate inner response is moral revulsion mirroring the divine response. From the perspective of the person who has committed abomination without conscience engagement: Jer 6:15 (vc=1680 — VCG-04) and Jer 8:12 (vc=1696 — VCG-04) show no immediate response — the conscience is wholly silenced and produces no shame or blushing. The immediate response therefore varies radically depending on whether conscience is functional (grief and recoil) or silenced (complete inner non-response).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence addresses the response to encountering the wicked person from the outside rather than the inner experience of adopting the characteristic from within. From the outside: the evidence shows immediate moral recoil and avoidance as the appropriate response. Psa 26:5 (VCG-03): "I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked" — deliberate moral separation as the will's first response. Psa 1:1 (VCG-04): the blessed person "walks not in the counsel of the wicked" — avoidance of the wicked person's counsel-register as the first step. Gen 18:25 (VCG-04) and Exo 23:7 (VCG-01) show the first response of the just judge: separation between wicked and righteous (the judicial impulse to name and distinguish). The response from the wicked person's own inner life to correction is the opposite: Pro 9:7 shows the immediate response is injury and abuse — wickedness resists its own naming.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Luk 7:47 — "she loved much" — the woman's love is the most immediate inner-being response to received forgiveness: the magnitude of forgiveness received produces a proportional love-response. Col 2:13 — "made alive" — the immediate inner response to forgiveness received is new life displacing prior death. Lev 16:30 — "you shall be clean before the Lord from all your sins" — the purity-status is the immediate declared condition following the atonement's completion. The immediate inner response thus ranges from the affective (love — Luk 7:47), through the vital (alive — Col 2:13), to the relational-status (clean — Lev 16:30).

**[CHAR-3]** E — From the perspective of those who encounter CHAR-3: the Pauline discourse evidences the complexity of reception. 2Cor 11:1 (context of VCG-02 corpus): Paul asks the Corinthians to "bear with him in a little foolishness" — the audience's immediate response to boasting is to perceive it as foolish or socially uncomfortable; 2Cor 11:16 (vc=33893, M08-C-VCG-02): Paul anticipates that even legitimate examined boasting will be received as foolishness. 1Cor 5:6 (vc=33903, M08-C-VCG-01): "your boasting is not good" — the community's internal boasting produces a discomfort addressed directly.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence addresses two types of encounter: encountering the command to abhor evil, and encountering the wicked person who embodies it. For the righteous community encountering the constitutionally evil: Rom 12:9 (vc=14417 — VCG-06) calls for "abhorring" evil — a deep moral revulsion as the first inner response. 1Pe 2:1 (vc=14369 — VCG-05) calls for immediately "putting away" malice as the first act of the community that receives the word. Jam 1:21 (vc=14368 — VCG-05) calls for stripping away rampant wickedness. The immediate response to the characteristic's presence is therefore a call to active repugnance and removal. For the constitutionally evil person encountering truth or testimony: Joh 7:7 (vc=14449 — VCG-04) shows the world hating the one who testifies that its works are evil — the immediate response of the constitutionally evil to exposure is hatred of the witness.

question_text: Across the verses, is that immediate response consistent or varied?

sample.text: **[CHAR-5]** E — The immediate response varies by VCG. In VCG-01 (dismissive inner attitude), the immediate response may be subtle — a gradual loss of confidence and standing. In VCG-02 (violent rejection), the response is acute wound. In VCG-03 (verbal attack), the immediate pull is toward retaliation, which 1Pe 3:9 specifically addresses.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence varies. Some verses focus on the dishonorer (Luk 18:2/4 — the judge's character trait); others on the dishonoured person's response (2Cor 6:8 — Paul's sustained integrity; Joh 8:49 — Jesus's redirection). No single consistent immediate response is described across the 15-verse corpus.

Consistent in direction: inner breaking followed by the impulse toward appeal. The form varies — acute crisis (2Ki 19:3), sustained lament (Psa 69), corporate appeal (Joel 2:17) — but the pattern holds.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Variable depending on the person's constitutional state. For the un-born-again person: the enslaving power holds and the response is continued sinning (Joh 8:34 — slavery through practice; Rom 6:2 — "live in it"). For the born-of-God person: the enslaving power is structurally resisted (1Jo 3:9 — "cannot keep on sinning"; 1Jo 5:18 — "does not keep on sinning"). For the endangered person within the community: 1Jo 5:16 — prayer and life given through intercession — the response available is communal-intercessory.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Consistent within each characteristic's primary mode; variable across the cluster. The collapse-withdrawal pattern is the most consistent (Chars 1, 2, 5). The evaluative-recoil pattern is consistent for functioning Char 4. The confidence-for-approach pattern is consistent for functioning Char 6. Variable dimension: within Char 1, the voluntary-bearing mode (M07-A-VCG-03) produces willed steadiness rather than collapse (Isa 50:7 — "I have set my face like a flint"); within Char 5, Bartimaeus's cloak-throwing (Mar 10:50) is decisive agency rather than collapse. These volitional-override patterns represent the cluster's resilience capacity — where the will is engaged toward a stronger referent, shame's default collapse-response is transcended.

question_text: What does the characteristic produce in the inner being over time in this verse — what states, qualities, capacities, or orientations does it establish? Record it, or record none.

sample.text: **[CHAR-2]** E — The corpus for CHAR-2 is primarily an act-and-remedy corpus — it does not evidence sustained-effect trajectories in the way CHAR-1 (escalating sinning) does. The Levitical framework (Lev 4:2; Num 15:27/28) addresses individual occurrences rather than a pattern that produces inner-being states over time. The sustained-effect evidence that is present: Lev 4:3 ("the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people") shows that repeated priestly sinning would accumulate communal guilt — a sustained inner-being effect on the community (collective guilt-load). The Eze 43/45 purification corpus suggests that sacred spaces accumulate defilement over time requiring periodic remediation — a sustained ritual-contamination dynamic. Within the personal-moral register, the corpus is predominantly episodic rather than developmental.

Scope is wide but with a clearer primary location: heart as the seat of the quality (1Ki 8:18), with somatic consequence (Pro 17:22), moral faculty expression (632-002), and volitional faculty expression (632-003). The characteristic is constitutional — it shapes across the whole inner person rather than operating through one faculty alone.
Pro 16:23 (VCG03 corpus): judicious speech, restraint of impulse, teachability. Psa 111:10 (VCG09 anchor): covenantal fidelity.

Hos 6:3 (VCG04 anchor) corpus: deepening covenantal relationship with God. Pro 1:7 (VCG06 anchor) corpus: accumulated inner wisdom that is guarded and transmitted. VCG08 (Rom 8:28): settled inner conviction that provides stability.

Sustained covetous jealousy produces physical deterioration: Pro 14:30 (M02-E-VCG-04) names envy as rotting the bones — the sustained inner state of covetous jealousy destroys the person who harbours it. Pro 27:4 calls it the most irresistible and devastating of destructive passions.

question_text: How does the sustained effect differ from the immediate response (T1.5)?

sample.text: Uniformly yes across all sub-groups. The immediate response is a specific act or opening; the sustained effect is a constituted quality or orientation formed over time. The pattern is consistent across the cluster: encounter/reception → immediate cognitive/volitional/affective opening → sustained formation of character/orientation/capacity. This is a cluster-level pattern.

Across M01, the sustained effect consistently differs from the immediate response in the dimension of scale and constitutional depth. The immediate response is situational; the sustained effect is formative. This is a significant cluster-level finding: fear is not merely an episodic experience but a formative characteristic whose sustained operation shapes the inner person over time.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The immediate response (T1.5.1) is primarily relational opening — the moment of humbling produces immediate access to God's mercy or divine exaltation. The sustained effect differs in kind: it is characterological rather than eventive. Phili4:12 ("I have *learned* the secret of facing… being brought low") evidences that sustained navigation of the lowliness condition produces a *learned* stability — a cultivated inner quality rather than a moment of opening. Col3:12 (humility as a "put-on" character-garment) evidences that sustained voluntary humbling shapes the whole inner person's character-wardrobe, not merely producing isolated moments of divine access. Pro11:2 (humility → wisdom) evidences that sustained humility produces a deepened inner capacity (wisdom) rather than merely repeated moments of receptivity. The sustained effect is the characterological deposit of the repeated inner act.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Yes, consistently across all five characteristics. The immediate experience of each M08 characteristic does not register as dangerous to the possessor: CHAR-1's initial experience is confident aspiration; CHAR-2's is energised volitional assertion; CHAR-3's VCG-01 form is the satisfaction of social recognition; CHAR-4's is the felt competence of knowledge; CHAR-5's is the secure ease of structural power. The sustained effect is comprehensively different: progressive deepening toward blindness, collapse, and judgment. This gap between initial experience (positive, confident, self-affirming) and sustained consequence (catastrophic) is a cluster-level feature of M08 — the cluster's characteristics are systematically self-concealing in their initial form. This is the analytical basis for why the wisdom tradition's structural-law approach (Pro 16:18: "pride goes before destruction") is necessary — the person experiencing pride cannot perceive the consequential trajectory from inside it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Consistently across the cluster, the sustained effect differs significantly from the immediate response. The immediate response is acute (collapse, withdrawal, recoil); the sustained effect is formative (identity-shaping, conscience-forming or conscience-degrading, relational-access determining). The most significant cluster-level observation: the same immediate response (shame's collapse) can produce very different sustained outcomes depending on whether it is received as corrective, refused, voluntarily borne, or imposed unjustly. The determining factor — the will's orientation — brings the cluster's primary volitional theme back as the decisive long-term differentiator.

question_text: Under what inner conditions does the characteristic take hold or operate rightly?

sample.text: **[CHAR-5]** E — (1) **Wisdom in the heart** — Pro 2:10 ("wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul") — the prior dwelling of wisdom enables Pleasure in knowledge; (2) **Covenant faithfulness** — the ni.cho.ach corpus consistently: Lev 26:31 (God will not smell the aromas of the unfaithful) — covenant obedience is the enabling condition for worship-Pleasure; (3) **Purity of speech and thought** — Pro 15:26 (gracious words are pure, contrasted with wicked thoughts) — inner purity enables genuine speech-Pleasure; (4) **Seeking after God** — Psa 27:4 (the one seeking to dwell in God's house and gaze on his beauty) — active seeking is the enabling posture for divine-Pleasure reception; (5) **Inner openness** — Pro 22:18 ("pleasant if you keep them within you") — inward reception of wisdom's words enables their pleasantness to be felt.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The inner condition enabling CHAR-3's avoidance is the inner faculty of regard (entrepō): "fearing God and respecting man" (Luk 18:2) — the worth-recognition capacity operating properly. For the dishonoured, grounded knowledge of one's standing before God enables receiving external dishonour without inner displacement (2Cor 6:8 — Paul's sustained integrity).

Several enabling conditions emerge from the corpus. (1) Genuine relational bond: grief arises from and requires a genuine attachment — the greater the bond, the greater the grief (David's grief for Absalom surpasses calculation, 2Sa 18:33 — M03-A-VCG-01). (2) Moral and empathic responsiveness: those who genuinely receive grief are those whose inner being is calibrated to the weight of loss and moral failure — the sighing ones in Eze 9:4 (M03-E-VCG-01) are those whose conscience-driven inner response distinguishes them for divine marking. (3) Humility and openness to God: penitential weeping requires a tender, humbled heart (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27 — M03-A-VCG-02). (4) Honest inner access: genuine grief requires that the inner person have access to its own state — Job's complaint pours out because he does not suppress it (Job 10:1 — M03-BOUNDARY). (5) Awareness of loss: grief requires that the person know what has been or is being lost — Rachel weeps inconsolably because she knows the children are gone (Jer 31:15 — M03-A-VCG-01).

F-007 and Q028 answers establish this comprehensively. The NT names multiple inner-being access-postures:

1. **Repentance** — Mar 1:4, Luk 24:47, Act 2:38, Act 5:31: named as the primary inner-being access-posture for forgiveness. An inner turning away from sin and toward God.
2. **Faith** — Act 10:43: "everyone who believes receives forgiveness through his name." Belief/faith as the inner orientation through which forgiveness is received.
3. **Confession** — 1Jo 1:9: "if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive." The inner acknowledgement made verbal.
4. **Prayer/intercession** — group 5379-002 corpus: the posture of radical dependence, calling on God's character. Dan 9:19 as the paradigm.
5. **Calling upon God** — Psa 86:5: "to all who call upon you" — the access-posture is simply calling; no further condition named.

The data is careful to note (F-007): "These are access-postures, not merit-conditions. They name the inner orientation through which forgiveness is received, not the basis on which it is earned."

In the **OT cultic mode** (group 5379-001): participation in the prescribed ritual — no specific inner-being posture named beyond the ritual act. The mechanism is external.

The enabling inner condition for genuine fellowship is desire oriented toward the fellowship object (SP-062-001 — desire as the inner motivating state directing fellowship). Psa 119:63 is a declared volitional alignment; Phili 3:10 is an aspirational pursuit. The inner condition enabling genuine fellowship is a will oriented toward the object — not mere proximity, not external compliance, but genuine desire-directed alignment. OBS-062-028, OBS-062-048, OBS-062-055.

question_text: Under what inner conditions is the characteristic blocked, distorted, resisted, or not taken up — including, where the evidence shows it, distortion or interference by another spirit (adversarial or angelic)?

sample.text: **[B — Moral Uprightness]** The demand for smooth things instead of what is right (Isa 30:10, VSG 1214-001). Crookedness — the habitual orientation toward devious paths (Pro 2:15).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The verse evidence evidences three blocking conditions. First, deliberate inner self-lowering: Psa 131:1 (vc=34059, M08-A1-VCG-03; vc=34224, M08-A2-VCG-01) — "my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me" — the active, chosen restraint of the heart's and eyes' upward movement blocks CHAR-1's entry. Second, reverent fear of God: Rom 11:20 (vc=60876, M08-A4-VCG-01) — Paul warns against becoming high-minded and commands: "do not become proud, but fear" — the fear of God as the active counter-disposition that prevents elevation of self. Third, humility/lowliness of spirit (M09): Jam 4:6 (vc=33931, M08-A4-VCG-01); 1Pe 5:5 (vc=33934, M08-A4-VCG-01) — "God... gives grace to the humble" — the humble inner posture draws the opposite of what CHAR-1 draws (divine grace vs divine opposition).

Inner closure is produced (not blocked) by wealth operating on the person without the countervailing conditions of character, trust, and humility. The block on inner closure is those countervailing conditions — having them prevents inner closure. For hardness: cha.mal (pity) is the inner capacity that wealth erodes; its presence is the block on hardness.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Three blocking conditions. (1) *Self-deception through prosperity*: Hos 12:8 — "in all my labors they cannot find in me iniquity or sin" — material success produces a false sense of moral clearance; (2) *Suppression of the record*: Psa 32:5 — "I did not cover my iniquity" (the positive) implies that covering is the blocking condition; Jer 16:10 — the people's inability to identify their sin shows a suppression that blocks reception; (3) *Hardened face*: Isa 3:9 — "they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it" — conscience has been so thoroughly suppressed that the record no longer produces shame; the blocking condition has become permanent display without awareness of its gravity.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The structural opposite (M08 — proud self-display) implies the primary blocking condition: when the person's inner orientation is toward self-promotion, status-assertion, and performance of worth, the settled inner gravity of semnotēs cannot take hold. Proud self-display (M08 register) blocks the self-possession and non-assertive gravity that semnotēs names. Additionally, frivolousness or lack of moral seriousness would prevent the characteristic from forming — the person whose manner is light or self-trivialising cannot carry the sober weighty gravity of semnotēs.

question_text: What is the inner-being state of the person in whom the characteristic is present but does not take hold?

sample.text: The person who encounters despair-circumstances and does not receive it is described in Isa 57:10 — wearied but found new strength, "and so were not faint." The non-despair state in the face of genuine cause for despair is wearied-but-renewed perseverance. In 2Cor 4:8 — "perplexed but not driven to despair" — the state is pressed but held.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Hos 12:8 names it: "I am rich... they cannot find in me iniquity" — the inner state is wealthy self-sufficiency generating false moral confidence. Psa 36:2 — "flatters himself in his own eyes" — the inner state is proud self-deception. Job 31:33 — "if I have concealed my transgressions... by hiding my iniquity in my heart" — the alternative to honest disclosure is conscious inner concealment; the person knows the iniquity but buries it deliberately. The denier's inner state thus has two forms: unconscious self-deception (Psa 36:2 — cannot see or hate the iniquity) and conscious concealment (Job 31:33 — hiding it in the heart).

**[CHAR-3]** S — The evidence does not extensively describe the inner state of the person who encounters worth-denial directed at them but does not receive it as a blow to their standing. Silent on this specific prompt.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The person who encounters the wicked but does not adopt the characteristic maintains deliberate moral separation and inner integrity. Psa 26:5 (VCG-03) is the clearest evidence: "I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked" — the maintenance of moral separation requires an active internal stance of refusal. Psa 1:1 (VCG-04) describes the blessed person as defined by what they refuse to enter. The wicked's social-corrosive power (Num 16:26 — VCG-04 — "proximity risks being swept away") indicates that the person who does not receive the characteristic must actively distance; the inner state is one of maintained integrity against a contagious force. 2Ch 19:2 (VCG-03) warns that helping the wicked even without adopting their wickedness draws divine displeasure — the inner state of the non-receiver must include practical separation, not merely internal distinction.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The person who cannot receive CHAR-4's corrective is the one whose evaluative standard has been replaced by self-worship or earthly orientation. Phili 3:19's "their end is destruction" names this person's trajectory. The inverted conscience does not receive CHAR-4's corrective signal because the signal itself has been reinterpreted by the corrupted standard.
